tier_reason: BENCH-rocks.txt is Dgraph's own log with public code (badger-bench bench_test.go, populate/, store/store.go) and states the i3.large instance plus the RocksDB v5.1.4 build (USE_RTTI=1 make shared_lib, in the README). It gives no CPU model and no Go version, so it cannot be A, and a first-party run with partial methodology is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not stated anywhere in badger-bench's BENCH-rocks.txt, README or the 2017 blog post (the record's 'Go 1.8' is unsupported). RocksDB v5.1.4 was built with `export USE_RTTI=1 && make shared_lib` (badger-bench README) and called from Go through cgo bindings (badger-bench rdb/).
corrections.hardware: Amazon EC2 i3.large dedicated instance: 2 cores, 16GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD (fio measured ~93K random-read IOPS at 4K block size); CPU model not stated
corrections.caveats: This is Dgraph's own 2017 benchmark against RocksDB v5.1.4, and the badger-bench repo has been archived (last commit 2019-09-20). Tuning was asymmetric: RocksDB was opened read-only with default options, a 16-bit bloom filter and the default block cache, called through cgo, while Badger ran with TableLoadingMode=LoadToRAM so its LSM tree sat in memory. Badger did not win every test. Loading 250M x 128B was slower with Badger (45:26.56 vs 39:10.78 for RocksDB), and the blog post says Badger can be 2-3x slower to load 16-byte values. Go version and CPU model are not stated.

notes: The numbers match the page: 118982 vs 32361 ns/op and the 3.67x headline, plus 1:18:08 vs 17:09.66 for loading 75M x 1KB (~4.55x, derived). The page shows the same trend at 1KB reads (156694 vs 37053 ns/op) and 16KB reads (215171 vs 40178). The original blog URLs (blog.dgraph.io/post/badger/, dgraph.io/blog/post/badger/) return 404, so I read an archive.org copy. The default branch's last commit is 2026-09-21; 2026-09-23 is pushed_at.

tier_reason: InfluxData, which is independent of HyperLevelDB, published this benchmark. It compares HyperLevelDB with LevelDB, RocksDB and LMDB, describes the method, and gives numbers in a results-table image, with raw logs in a linked gist. The page gives no compiler, flags, CPU model or benchmark-code link, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Writing 100M values took 10m45.41s with HyperLevelDB vs 36m8.29s with LevelDB (~3.36x faster, derived from page data) and 21m18.60s with RocksDB. HyperLevelDB lost the other steps: querying 100M values took 13m49.01s vs 2m55.37s for LevelDB (~4.7x slower, derived from page data), and it was also slower than LevelDB on delete (6m0.38s vs 3m47.64s) and compaction (6m33.36s vs 3m59.87s).
corrections.caveats: This is a 2014 benchmark on a 2-core, 4GB DigitalOcean droplet. The author says settings were not tuned per engine, and the page gives no compiler, flags or CPU model. HyperLevelDB wins only on writes and is the slowest engine for range queries. The last three rows of the results image (Query 50M, Write 50M, DB size) match the 30M run in the linked gist, not the 100M run. In the gist's 3M-value SSD run, HyperLevelDB writes were slower than LevelDB's (21.0s vs 18.0s).

notes: The record said the page gives no numbers, but they are in the results image (grid.png). I replaced the claim with the numbers and recorded the losses on reads, deletes and compaction. Metadata checks out: BSD-3-Clause, 464 stars, last commit 2016-02-16, abandoned; not a GitHub fork, but conceptually derived from google/leveldb.

tier_reason: The '30x faster than SQLite' figure appears only in the README tagline, with no methodology or results. The public XCTest comparison (Tests/CacheAdvanceTests/SQLitePerformanceComparisonTests.swift) has no recorded numbers, compiler or hardware. That is first-party and short of A, so C.

corrections.caveats: The 30x figure is a first-party README claim from April 2020 (commit 6ae0a74 changed an earlier '15x faster while utilizing 40% less memory than SQLite'). The benchmark_url test file measures but prints no stored results and gives no hardware or Xcode/Swift version, and performance tests are disabled on GitHub Actions. The SQLite baseline is naive: every append runs a SELECT COUNT(*), prepares a fresh INSERT and commits it on its own under SQLite's default durability, with no batching, prepared-statement reuse or WAL. CacheAdvance's append path shows no fsync, so the comparison favors it.

notes: The benchmark_url shows the SQLite comparison code but not the 30x number, which is only in the README tagline. The category 'embedded-kv' fits loosely: this is an append-only log/message cache. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 51 stars, last commit 2026-06-23, active.
